summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar; Sanjay Barua; Nitin Khandelwal; Kundan Kumar Chaubey; Ram Kumar; Krishan Dutt; Yogesh Chander; Thachamvally Riyesh; Vir Shoor Singh; Bhupendra Nath
summary.executive_summary: This study identifies the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) as a critical host factor facilitating replication of paramyxoviruses, specifically Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study identifies the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) as a critical host factor facilitating replication of paramyxoviruses, specifically Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors utilized Thapsigargin, a specific SERCA inhibitor, to demonstrate that blocking SERCA activity significantly reduces viral replication without causing cytotoxicity at the tested concentration. Mechanistic assays revealed that SERCA inhibition specifically impairs viral entry and the proper subcellular localization of viral proteins, preventing their transport from the cytoplasm to the cell surface. Furthermore, the study observed that viral infection itself induces SERCA expression, which can be blocked by the inhibitor. A notable finding is that while PPRV remained sensitive to the inhibitor, long-term passage of NDV in the presence of Thapsigargin led to the emergence of a partially resistant mutant, suggesting viruses can evolve to bypass host factor dependencies. These findings position SERCA as a promising target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics against paramyxoviruses.

Research Context
Antiviral strategies have classically relied upon targeting essential proteins of the pathogens. High mutation rate in viral genome allows the virus to become resistant to antiviral drugs. The rise in incidence of drug resistance has prompted a shift in the development of novel antiviral drugs. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that are highly dependent on host. Proviral host factors may serve as targets for development of novel antiviral therapeutics. The role of these Ca2+-ATPases in virus replication is only beginning to be appreciated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study screened a library of kinase and phosphate inhibitors for their antiviral potential against paramyxovirus. Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) was identified as one of the candidate that blocked NDV and PPRV replication. The study aims to provide mechanistic insights into the potential roles of SERCA in facilitating paramyxovirus replication. The hypothesis is that SERCA facilitates paramyxovirus replication, primarily in mediating viral entry and localization of viral proteins. It is hypothesized that targeting SERCA will block paramyxovirus replication at the level of viral entry.

Methodological Details
Vero (African green-monkey kidney), 293T (human embryonic kidney), HeLa and goat kidney cells were grown in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium. Thapsigargin (SERCA inhibitor) was procured from Sigma (Catalog Number-T9033, Steinheim, Germany). Thapsigargin is a non-competitive inhibitor of SERCA. Cytooxicity of Thapsigargin was analyzed in MTT assay. Vero/MDBK cells were infected with respective viruses at MOI=0.1 in the presence of 0.5 µM Thapsigargin or vehicle control (DMSO). Viral titers were determined by plaque assay. HeLa/goat kidney cells were transfected in 24 well plates, in triplicates with either 1 µg of empty vector (pCR3) or with a plasmid expressing SERCA2 (pCR3-SERCA2). Virus step-specific assays (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis and budding) employed in this study were conducted as previously described. PPRV and NDV were sequentially passaged (70 passages) in Vero cells in the presence of either 0.25 µM Thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO (vehicle control).

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin at concentrations from 0.00064 µM to 2 µM did not significantly affect the cell viability even when incubated in cell cultures for 96 h. A non-cytotoxic concentration (0.5 µM) of Thapsigargin was used thereafter. Overexpression of SERCA2 not only facilitated NDV/PPRV replication, but also rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on virus replication. PPRV infection of Vero cells resulted in enhanced SERCA2 expression. A significant induction in SERCA2 expression was observed at 3 hpi, which remained at the peak level between 24-72 hpi. The inhibitor was applied at different time post-infection and the virus released into the supernatant was quantified by plaque assay. Thapsigargin was not found to affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis and budding. Thapsigargin treatment resulted in reduced NDV and PPRV titers suggesting that SERCA inhibitor blocks paramyxovirus entry. Thapsigargin treatment showed defective localization in ~70% of the cells, as compared to DMSO control wherein this proportion was 10-30 %.

Key Results
Thapsigargin significantly inhibited paramyxovirus viz; NDV, PPRV replication. Thapsigargin did not exhibit any virucidal effect on any of the prototype virus tested. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on virus replication. Virus infection induced SERCA expression in Vero cells which could be blocked by Thapsigargin. The highest inhibition was observed when the inhibitor was applied 30 min before infection. Thapsigargin did not exhibit any inhibitory effect on virus replication if it was applied at 10 hpi. Thapsigargin treatment showed defective localization in ~70% of the cells, as compared to DMSO control wherein this proportion was 10-30 %. NDV, when passaged sequentially in presence of a SERCA inhibitor (Thapsigargin) did not generate a completely resistant phenotype against Thapsigargin, even upon 70 passages. Significant resistance was observed at P35 (~100 fold-inhibition compared to ~10,000 fold inhibition at zero passage). All PPRVs (P0, P70-Thapsigargin and P70-Control) revealed similar sensitivity to Thapsigargin even at passage level 70.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Targeting host factors could have a significant impact on multiple virus genotypes (strain/serotype) and provide broad spectrum inhibition. SERCA may present as a novel target for antiviral drug development. This is the first documented example where a paramyxovirus significantly bypassing its dependency on a cellular factor that is targeted by a small molecule inhibitor. One possible mechanism underlying acquisition of drug resistance is due to change in host factor requirement. We have provided strong evidence for SERCA as a crucial host factor in facilitating optimal paramyxoviral replication.

Contradictions And Limitations
In immunofluorescence assay, we could not observe a perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins. The co-immunoprecipitation assay to analyze the interaction between SERCA/virus was unsuccessful. Therefore, in this study, we could not determine any direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins. Fluctuations in the overall viral titers and hence variation in fold inhibition was observed. Which viral proteins(s) have acquired mutations upon prolonged passage in presence of SERCA inhibitor remains to be determined.

Claims
SERCA is a critical host factor required for paramyxovirus replication. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited paramyxovirus viz; NDV, PPRV replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on virus replication. Thapsigargin did not exhibit any virucidal effect on any of the prototype virus tested. SERCA may present as a novel target for antiviral drug development.
SERCA inhibition specifically blocks viral entry and proper subcellular localization of viral proteins. Thapsigargin treatment resulted in reduced NDV and PPRV titers suggesting that SERCA inhibitor blocks paramyxovirus entry. Thapsigargin treatment showed defective localization in ~70% of the cells. Thapsigargin was not found to affect virus attachment, RNA synthesis and budding. SERCA is required for proper localization of the viral proteins (cytoplasm to the cell surface).
Viruses can acquire resistance to host-targeting antiviral agents under selection pressure. Significant resistance was observed at P35 (~100 fold-inhibition compared to ~10,000 fold inhibition at zero passage). All PPRVs (P0, P70-Thapsigargin and P70-Control) revealed similar sensitivity to Thapsigargin even at passage level 70. This is the first documented example where a paramyxovirus significantly bypassing its dependency on a cellular factor.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on virus replication. Control-passaged viruses did not exhibit any significant resistance against Thapsigargin even upon 70 passages.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1a and 1b show Thapsigargin did not significantly affect cell viability at concentrations from 0.00064 µM to 2 µM. Fig. 2a and 2b demonstrate that overexpression of SERCA2 facilitated NDV/PPRV replication and rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin. Fig. 3a shows PPRV infection resulted in enhanced SERCA2 expression at 3 hpi, peaking between 24-72 hpi. Fig. 4a and 4b show the magnitude of viral inhibition gradually decreased when the inhibitor was applied later post-infection. Fig. 6c and 6d quantify that Thapsigargin treatment showed defective localization in ~70% of the cells compared to 10-30% in DMSO control. Fig. 7a and 7b show that NDV acquired significant resistance at P35 but not complete resistance even at P70.

Three Takeaways
SERCA is a crucial host factor facilitating paramyxovirus replication and a candidate drug target. Thapsigargin specifically inhibits viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins. Viruses like NDV can acquire resistance to host-targeting inhibitors, though PPRV did not.
